items.title: Who Is Investing in the Next Generation?
items.excerpt: Last year, I spoke to a room full of Year 11 students about career paths. There were plenty of bright mathematics students. Exactly the sort of people who, not that long ago, might have seen actuarial science as an obvious career. I expected at least one of them to mention becoming an actuary. Not one did. That stayed with me. Around the same time, I read the now famous substack on the quiet decline of Australia’s life actuarial market. It articulated something many of us working in the industry have been feeling for years. The Australian life insurance industry isn’t just changing. I wonder whether it’s also quietly underinvesting in one of its most important long-term assets. Its future capability. An asset you won’t find on the balance sheet I’ve written previously about the idea of an Invisible Balance Sheet . Every company carefully manages the assets it can measure—capital, cash, technology and expenses. But every business also depends on assets that never appear in its financial statements. Trust. Institutional knowledge. Relationships. Culture. Leadership. And perhaps the most important of all... The next generation of talent. The life insurance industry spends a lot of time thinking about capital adequacy. I’m starting to wonder whether we should spend just as much time thinking about capability adequacy . Because capability compounds. Or disappears. The apprenticeship we never had to design For decades, the profession didn’t really have to think about how actuaries were developed. The system largely looked after itself. Universities produced graduates. Insurers and consultancies hired them. Graduates learned by doing. Reinsurers hired experienced actuaries. Over time, some moved into leadership and Chief Actuary roles... and eventually to the promised land of the previously limited liability of directorship. It wasn’t perfect. But it worked. items.title: The Chart That Changed an Industry
items.excerpt: In 2014, ASIC released REP 413, its landmark review of retail life insurance advice. The report would become one of the most influential documents in the history of Australia’s life insurance industry. It triggered industry reviews. It influenced government policy. It shaped public debate. And ultimately it laid the foundations for the Life Insurance Framework (LIF). Nearly a decade later, I have a simple question. Has anyone asked whether it actually worked? How We Got Here To understand whether LIF worked, we first need to acknowledge that it was trying to solve a genuine problem. This wasn’t a case of regulators waking up one morning and deciding to reduce commissions. LIF was the culmination of almost a decade of reform aimed at restoring trust in financial advice. The FOFA Era The Future of Financial Advice (FOFA) reforms fundamentally changed Australia’s approach to financial advice. Following high-profile investment scandals, the focus shifted towards conflicted remuneration. The philosophy was simple: Advice should be driven by client interests, not adviser incentives. Investment commissions were largely removed because policymakers believed embedded remuneration structures created conflicts that distorted advice outcomes. Life insurance, however, was treated differently. There was widespread recognition that life insurance advice wasn’t like investment advice. There was no investment balance from which fees could be deducted. No growing pool of assets to fund advice. The concern was that banning commissions entirely would dramatically reduce access to insurance advice. Life insurance commissions survived FOFA. But only just. ASIC concluded that approximately 37% of advice files reviewed failed to comply with ASIC’s requirements. items.title: Nobody Asks the Loss Ratio of a Couch
items.excerpt: Before we go any further, let’s start with a simple question. What is a loss ratio? A loss ratio is simply the amount an insurer pays in claims divided by the premiums it receives. If an insurer collects $100 in premiums and pays $50 in claims, it has a 50% loss ratio. Sounds simple enough. The problem is that many people assume a higher loss ratio automatically means better value. I’m not convinced that’s true. If I told you a life insurance company only paid out around 50 cents in claims for every dollar of premium it received, would you consider that good value? My first reaction was that it sounded poor value. In fact, many people would probably think it sounds terrible. After all, where did the other 50 cents go? Let’s consider the two pillars of Life Insurance in Australia – Retail and Group. In retail advised life insurance, insurers will often target a loss ratio somewhere around 45-50%. In group insurance, via superannuation funds, loss ratios can often target 80%. At first glance, that makes group insurance look like better value. If one product has a loss ratio of 80% and another has a loss ratio of 50%, surely the 80% product is better value? If you’re expecting an actuary to answer this question with a simple yes or no, you’re going to be disappointed. One of our favourite phrases is: “It depends.” I’ve spent much of my career pricing life insurance products, and one thing I’ve learned is that a 50% loss ratio doesn’t necessarily tell you much about profitability, and an 80% loss ratio doesn’t necessarily tell you much about value. I’ve seen products with lower loss ratios generate less profit than products with much higher loss ratios. The economics are far more complicated than many people realise. Why an 80% loss ratio isn’t always better than 50% The difference isn’t because retail insurers are making a fortune. The economics are simply different. items.excerpt: Actuaries Institute Maps the Generational Flow of Australia's $1 trillion Tax and Spending System Government spending follows a U-shaped pattern across Australians' lifetimes highest for children and those in their 80s while taxation peaks among working-age Australians. The report identifies several policy considerations for the future, including age-based tax and spending settings that better consider means, broadening the tax base, overall fiscal discipline and supporting asset accumulation at younger ages. items.excerpt: Recycling, greener diets, and other personal climate choices do not seem to distract people from supporting major environmental reforms. A four-year study of nearly 2,800 Australians found that these habits neither increased nor reduced later political engagement.

items.title: The Universe can outrun light without breaking Einstein’s rules
items.excerpt: Cosmic expansion allows distant galaxies to move away faster than light, while still letting us see ancient light they emitted when they were much closer. Eventually, accelerating expansion will push nearly every galaxy beyond our Local Group out of sight, making the Universe appear almost empty.

items.title: Venus may be tearing itself apart from within
items.excerpt: Scientists have uncovered new evidence that Venus may still be tearing itself apart from within. Advanced 3D simulations indicate that some of the planet's giant rift valleys formed relatively recently and could still be expanding. The results suggest Venus has a far more active interior than researchers once believed, challenging the long-held view of a geologically dormant world.

items.title: Scientists discover the Sun contains 55% more silver than expected
items.excerpt: A new analysis suggests the Sun holds far more silver than earlier estimates indicated. More advanced models of the solar atmosphere raised the calculated amount by 55 percent, bringing it into much closer agreement with ancient meteorites. The technique may also help scientists track the cosmic origins of silver and other heavy elements.

items.title: Graphene nanoribbons survive gamma radiation, revealing potential sensors for fusion reactors
items.excerpt: University of Arizona researchers have demonstrated a promising new application for graphene nanoribbons, a nanoscale semiconductor material with the potential to withstand extreme environments. The team's findings could help clear a key hurdle to bringing fusion energy to the electric grid.

items.title: Climate change reshapes waterborne disease risks as pathogens respond differently, review finds
items.excerpt: Climate change is altering the spread of waterborne diseases around the world, according to a comprehensive review published today in Nature Reviews Microbiology. The publication is the most up-to-date, comprehensive analysis examining how climate change influences waterborne diseases.
